---
title: "Serverless Interactive Reporting"
subtitle: "Quarto and Shinylive: interactive reports and apps without a server"
---

A 2-hour, hands-on workshop introducing **Quarto** and **Shinylive** for serverless interactive
reporting. All content is in English. Start with the [slides](slides/slides.html), then follow
the labs in order.

::: callout-tip
**Want to follow along?** [Download the workshop material](material.zip) (ZIP archive) to get
all the code, examples, and data on your own machine, no git needed.

- **Windows:** right-click the ZIP, choose *Extract All*, then open the `shinylive-quarto` folder.
- **macOS:** double-click the ZIP to unzip it, then open the `shinylive-quarto` folder.

Open the extracted folder as a project in **RStudio** (File, New Project, Existing Directory) or
**Positron** (File, Open Folder), then work through the labs in order.
:::

## The one idea

Shinylive output is **static**: the host serves files, and the reader's browser runs the R via
webR/WebAssembly. No server, no data transit, no hosting cost. The corollary: your code is
public, your packages must have WASM builds, and your data must stay modest.

## Prerequisites

A recent **R** (4.x), **Quarto CLI** (this material targets v1.10+), and an IDE (RStudio or
Positron) are enough for the first half. Install these R packages (e.g. with
`install.packages(c("shiny", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "readr", "shinylive", "httpuv", "gt"))`):

| Package | Purpose | WASM-safe? |
|---|---|---|
| `shiny` | UI + reactive server (the app framework) | yes |
| `dplyr` | data wrangling in the penguins app and labs | yes |
| `ggplot2` | plotting app and report figures | yes |
| `readr` | read the bundled `penguins.csv` | yes |
| `gt` | tables in the slide deck (optional, deck build only) | no |
| `shinylive` | export apps/reports to run in the browser | no (build-time) |
| `httpuv` | serve an exported site locally (`runStaticServer`) | no |
| `renv` | pin package versions for reproducible exports (Lab 3 stretch) | no |

WASM-safe packages are the ones that also run **inside** a `{shinylive-r}` block in the reader's
browser; the others are used on the host only. `palmerpenguins` is used in the example report's
live widget (also WASM-safe). `install.packages()` works for all of the above; Quarto extensions
(`quarto-ext/shinylive`) are installed per-project with `quarto add`.

## Deploying on your own

Everything hinges on one distinction:

| | Static host | Non-static (server) host |
|---|---|---|
| What it does | Serves **files** (HTML, JS, CSS, WASM) | Runs a **program** that computes for each request |
| Example | GitHub Pages, Netlify, Quarto Pub, any web server | shinyapps.io, Posit Connect, your own R server |
| Cost | Usually free | Server + maintenance |
| Can run Shiny? | Yes, **in the browser** via webR | Yes, traditionally server-side |
| Packages | Only WASM builds | Anything installable on the server |
| Secrets | Impossible (code is public) | Kept server-side |

A Shinylive app or report is **static**: the host hands the reader a pile of files and does
nothing else. The reader's browser executes the R. This is why the same output works on free
static hosts.

### Quick publish (no workflow needed)

From a Quarto project or document folder, the native commands:

```bash
quarto publish gh-pages      # push rendered output to GitHub Pages
quarto publish netlify       # deploy a folder to Netlify
quarto publish quarto-pub    # free, public, Posit-hosted service
```

These are ideal for one-off or interactive publishing. For durable, repeatable deployments,
prefer a GitHub Actions workflow.

### Automating with GitHub Actions

The reference workflow is the reusable `deploy-app.yaml` from `posit-dev/r-shinylive`
([view the source](https://github.com/posit-dev/r-shinylive/blob/actions-v1/.github/workflows/deploy-app.yaml)).
It checks out the repo, installs R and the app's packages (via `renv`), runs
`shinylive::export(".", "site")`, uploads `site/` as a Pages artifact, and deploys it on push.

For a standalone **app** repo, add `.github/workflows/deploy-app.yaml` based on that workflow. For
a Quarto **report** repo, the pattern is the same but you `quarto render` the report instead of
exporting an app, then deploy the output folder to Pages (or simply run `quarto publish
gh-pages`).

**GitHub Pages setup (one time):** push the repo, then **Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub
Actions**. The workflow needs `pages: write` and `id-token: write` permissions to deploy.

### Don't forget the service worker

Include the service worker as a project resource, or collaborators may see a blank page:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    resources:
      - shinylive-sw.js
```

### Offline / private sharing

Render locally, zip the output folder, and send it. The recipient unzips and double-clicks the
HTML: the interactive content runs in their browser, entirely offline and on no server.
